a: The church of God that lives as a resident alien in Rome
t: A letter from a church, not a person
p: The letter names no writer. One church writes to another; tradition later gave it Clement's name.
b: The greeting names two churches and no person. Lake: the letter "clearly claims to be not the letter of a single person but of a church", though "tradition, however, has always ascribed it to Clement", whom the early lists of bishops make the third or fourth bishop of Rome; he sees "no reason for rejecting this tradition". The opening copies Paul's greeting to the same city's church, "To the church of God that is in Corinth, those made holy ... called as saints" (1 Corinthians 1:2), and the letter will name that earlier letter outright (47:1). The church at Rome speaks as "we" throughout.

a: lives as a resident alien in Rome
p: Greek paroikeō: to live somewhere as a foreigner without citizen rights. The church's true home is elsewhere.
b: A paroikos was a resident foreigner, living in a city without its citizenship. The Greek Genesis uses it for Abraham in Egypt and in Canaan (Genesis 12:10; Genesis 17:8), and 1 Peter calls believers "resident aliens and temporary residents" (1 Peter 2:11; 1 Peter 1:17). From this word comes the later "parish" (Greek paroikia). The same greeting opens Polycarp to the Philippians and the Martyrdom of Polycarp. So the church of God does not belong to Rome or Corinth; it lives in each for a time, with its citizenship in heaven (compare Philippians 3:20).

a: God Almighty
p: Pantokratōr, the Greek Bible's word for "the LORD of Armies", rare in the New Testament outside Revelation.
b: Lightfoot notes that pantokratōr, "ruler of all", is the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew title "the LORD of Armies", apparently not a classical word, and that outside Revelation the New Testament has it only once, where Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament (2 Corinthians 6:18). 1 Clement uses it often (2:3; 8:5 "almighty will"; 32:4; 56:6; 60:4; 62:2), and the Latin omnipotens carried it into the creeds. The site renders it "the Almighty", as in Revelation 1:8.

a: May grace and peace from God Almighty be multiplied to you
p: A greeting with the wish "be multiplied", as in 1 and 2 Peter and Jude.
b: Paul greets with "grace to you and peace" (1 Corinthians 1:3). The verb "may it be multiplied" (plēthyntheiē) is the form of 1 Peter 1:2, 2 Peter 1:2 and Jude 1:2 ("Mercy to you, and peace, and love: may they be multiplied"), and of Nebuchadnezzar's letter in the Greek Daniel (Daniel 4:1). Lightfoot points to Jude. Peace is the word this letter will end on (65:2) and the goal it argues for throughout (19:2).

a: struck us suddenly, one after another
p: Lightfoot read the misfortunes as the persecution under Domitian, about AD 95-96. Lake warns how little is known of it.
b: The letter does not say what hit the church at Rome. Lightfoot read the words as an exact description of the persecution under Domitian: capricious, with Christians charged "from time to time on various paltry charges", unlike Nero's single onslaught, and he dated the letter to about AD 95 or 96, at the close of Domitian's reign or the start of Nerva's. Lake is more careful: if chapter 1 refers to Domitian's time the letter "can probably be dated as c. 96 A.D.; but we know very little about the alleged persecution in the time of Domitian", and it is "safest to say that it must be dated between 75 and 110 A.D.", with "general agreement" among critics for the last decade of the first century. The words could also mean troubles of other kinds.

a: the questions being argued among you
p: The Greek does not say Corinth wrote to Rome for advice. It means the matters in dispute at Corinth.
b: Lightfoot cautions against translations that say "the points about which you consulted us". Clement writes "among you" (par' hymin), not "from you", and ta epizētoumena means "the matters in dispute". So the text gives no sign that the Corinthians asked Rome to step in. Whether they did or not matters for how one reads Rome's role in the letter (see the chapter page). The letter itself says the news reached Rome by report (47:7).

a: the rebellion
p: Stasis, the Greek word for civil strife and faction, names the revolt at Corinth all through the letter.
b: In Greek political writing stasis is the worst thing that can happen to a city: faction, party strife, civil war. 1 Clement uses it for what happened at Corinth, where a few people removed elders from office (44:6; 47:6). The site renders it "rebellion" throughout, and keeps apart its partners: zēlos "jealousy", phthonos "envy" (3:2), eris "fighting" and schisma "split" (2:6), with homonoia "harmony" and eirēnē "peace" as the cure (20:11). The letter reads like a Greek speech on concord addressed to a church.

a: A handful of rash and headstrong people
p: The letter insists that a small group caused the trouble, and later names it "one or two persons".
b: Greek oliga prosōpa, "a few persons". The letter returns to this: the revolt is the work of "one or two persons" (47:6), and the call near the end is for its leaders to leave so that the flock may have peace with its elders (54:1-2). Rome writes to the whole church while blaming a few, which leaves room for the rest to return to the elders without shame.

a: self-controlled and forbearing
p: Epieikēs: the person who yields instead of pressing every right. The site keeps "forbearing" through the letter.
b: The Greek epieikēs describes someone who does not insist on the full letter of their rights, who gives way where strict justice would allow more. Clement praises it here in the old Corinth and calls for it again: the Lord Jesus taught "forbearance" (13:1). The site renders the word family "forbearing / forbearance" in all the Apostolic Fathers, as in its Titus 3:2: "They should be forbearing". On the other ways the site's New Testament renders it, see the note at 13:1.

a: your magnificent way of welcoming guests
p: Corinth was a port city on a busy crossing; Christians on the road stayed with the church there.
b: Clement praises the "magnificent" (megaloprepes) character of it, the word he uses again at 9:1-2. The word for the custom is philoxenia, "love of strangers", which the site renders "hospitality" (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2). Corinth sat on the isthmus between two harbors, and travelers between Rome and the East passed through it, as Paul, Aquila and Priscilla did (Acts 18:1-2). The praise prepares a theme: Abraham, Lot and Rahab are saved "because of faith and hospitality" (10:7; 11:1; 12:1).

a: knowledge
p: Gnōsis here is sound Christian understanding, not the "knowledge" of the later Gnostic groups.
b: The Greek is gnōsis. In the second century some groups made a secret "knowledge" the heart of salvation and were later called Gnostics. Nothing like that is in view here. Clement praises the Corinthians' understanding of the faith as "complete" and "sure", much as Paul thanks God that they were "made rich in every way, in all speech and all knowledge" (1 Corinthians 1:5), though he also warns that knowledge puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1).

a: the older people among you
p: Presbyteroi can mean "older people" or the church's "elders". Here the contrast with "the young" points to age.
b: The same Greek word names both. Lightfoot argues that here it means age: the church's own officers are already covered by "your leaders" (hēgoumenoi), and the next clause speaks of "the young", so Clement widens the honor to all who are older. Chapter 21 runs in the same order: leaders, the older, the young, the women (21:6). The site renders the office "elders" (44:5; 47:6) and age "older people", as here. In 3:3 the choice is harder (see the note there).

a: You instructed the women
p: The duties of wives here match the household codes of the New Testament letters.
b: Wives who love their husbands, stay within "the rule of submission" and manage the home with dignity: the list is close to Titus 2:4-5 and 1 Peter 3:1-6, and Clement repeats it in his own exhortation (21:6-8). Lightfoot notes that Polycarp later follows this wording (Polycarp to the Philippians 4:2, on wives who love their husbands). Such household rules were a common form in Greek ethics as well as in the churches.
r: Titus 2:4-5; 1 Peter 3:1-6; Ephesians 5:22-33; 21:6-8; Polycarp to the Philippians 4:2

a: humble
p: Tapeinophroneō, "to be lowly-minded", the virtue chapters 13-19 hold up against the revolt.
b: The verb tapeinophroneō and its noun tapeinophrosynē run through the letter (13:1, 3; 16:1-2, 17; 17:2; 19:1). The site's Philippians 2:3 renders the noun "with a lowly mind"; here the verb is "be humble". In Greek ethics "lowly" was often a slur, the mark of a slave. The Christian use makes it a virtue, modeled on Christ who "made himself low" (Philippians 2:8). Clement's point is pointed: the rebels exalted themselves (16:1); the cure is humility.

a: happier to give than to receive
t: A saying of the Lord in Acts
p: Echoes the saying Paul quotes in Acts 20:35, found in no Gospel.
b: Paul tells the Ephesian elders to "keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, 'Giving is more blessed than receiving.'" (Acts 20:35). Clement's phrase, "more gladly giving than receiving", is close, and Lake prints the reference in his margin. Lightfoot also notes Greek parallels, among them Seneca, who says a man errs if he receives a benefit more gladly than he repays it. The Acts saying is in no Gospel; see the topic on sayings of Jesus outside the Gospels. Clement uses the Acts formula itself at 13:1.

a: the supplies Christ gives for the journey
p: Ephodia were supplies for a journey; the Christian life is pictured as travel.
b: Ephodia are travel provisions, the food and money for a journey. Lightfoot takes it as "the provision ... for the journey of life" and compares Seneca and Epictetus, and 1 Timothy 6:8: "If we have food and covering, we will count that enough". The Corinthians were content with what they had. Codex Alexandrinus reads "the supplies God gives" (see the variant), which changes who "his words" and "his sufferings" refer to.

a: The Holy Spirit was poured out in full on everyone
p: The language of Joel and of Pentecost, now said of the church at Corinth in its good days.
b: "Poured out" is the verb of Joel's promise that God would pour out his Spirit on all people, taken up at Pentecost (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17) and in Titus 3:6. Clement says it of a whole local church at peace. Paul had written to the same church about the many gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:4-11); Clement links the Spirit not with the gifts but with peace and the wish to do good.

a: if you had sinned in anything without intending it
p: The law of Moses provided for sins committed unknowingly; the Corinthians prayed about them too.
b: Leviticus sets out offerings for one who "sins by mistake" (Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:27-28). The Corinthians did not wait for a priest; they lifted their hands in prayer, the common posture of prayer in the ancient world (1 Timothy 2:8). The point is their tender conscience: they worried even about sins they had not meant.

a: brotherhood
p: Adelphotēs, the whole family of believers, as in 1 Peter.
b: In the New Testament the word is found only in 1 Peter (1 Peter 2:17; 1 Peter 5:9). It pictures the church as one family. The Corinthians' struggle "day and night" was prayer for the whole family of believers, that the full number of God's chosen would be saved (compare Revelation 6:11).

a: Every rebellion and every split
p: The two words name what has now happened at Corinth. Paul had warned the same church against splits.
b: Paul wrote to Corinth, "let there be no divisions among you" (1 Corinthians 1:10, Greek schismata), and listed "splits" among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20). Clement's portrait of the old Corinth is built to be the opposite of the present one: once every rebellion and split was hateful to them; now "a few" have stirred up both (1:1; 46:9).

a: ready for any good work
p: The same words as Titus 3:1.
b: Titus 3:1 asks believers "to stand ready for any good work"; Clement's Greek has nearly the same words, and Lake prints the reference in his margin. Whether Clement knew the letter to Titus is debated with the date of the Pastoral Letters; the phrase may also have been a common one in the churches.

a: Your way of life as citizens
p: Politeia, citizenship or civic life. Clement speaks of the church in the language of a city.
b: The noun politeia (here) and the verb politeuomai, "live as a citizen" (3:4; 6:1; 21:1; 44:6; 51:2; 54:4), come from polis, "city". Paul uses the verb the same way: "live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ" (Philippians 1:27). For Clement the church is like a well-ordered city whose laws are God's commands; rebellion is a crime against that city.

a: written on your heart's tablets
t: The heart as a writing tablet
p: An image from Proverbs, used again by Paul to the Corinthians.
b: Proverbs tells the student to "write them on your heart's tablet" (Proverbs 7:3; Proverbs 3:3), and Jeremiah promises a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). Paul told the same church that they were "a letter of Christ ... written not in ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on tablets that are hearts of flesh" (2 Corinthians 3:3). Lake's margin points to Proverbs 7.

a: The beloved one ate and drank
p: The Greek of the Song of Moses names Israel "the beloved one" where the Hebrew has the name Jeshurun.
b: The site's Deuteronomy 32:15 reads, from the Hebrew, "Jeshurun grew fat, and he kicked". The Septuagint gives the name Jeshurun as ho ēgapēmenos, "the beloved one". Clement quotes the Greek loosely and in his own order (ate and drank, grew broad, grew fat, kicked), and he applies it to Corinth: success and comfort made the church restless. The formula "what is written came true" treats the Song of Moses as a warning that keeps being fulfilled.

a: jealousy and envy
p: Zēlos and phthonos, the theme of chapters 3-6. The site keeps one English word for each.
b: Zēlos can be good "zeal" (2 Corinthians 7:11) or bad rivalry; in 1 Clement it is always the bad kind, and the site renders it "jealousy", as in 1 Corinthians 13:4 ("Love is not jealous") and Galatians 5:20. Phthonos is "envy", resentment of another's good (Galatians 5:21; Matthew 27:18). Clement uses the pair at 3:2, 4:7, 4:13 and 5:2, and "jealousy" runs as a refrain through every verse of 4:7-6:4. Paul had diagnosed the same church: "there is jealousy and strife among you" (1 Corinthians 3:3).

a: the young against the elders
p: Presbyteroi again: "the old" or "the elders"? Here both senses seem meant, since the young rose against officers.
b: The line adapts the Greek of Isaiah 3:5, where "the child" will push against "the old man" (Greek presbytēs) and "the dishonored against the honored". Clement changes the word to presbyteroi, the title of the officers who were removed at Corinth (44:5-6; 47:6). The site chooses by context: since the other pairs are about standing (honor, name, sense) and the letter's complaint is a revolt against elders, the site says "the elders" here, against the age reading of 1:3. The young may have led the revolt, or "young" may describe newer members.

a: death came into the world
p: Clement quotes the Wisdom of Solomon, which blames "the devil's envy". He puts "jealousy" in its place.
b: The Wisdom of Solomon, a book Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include, says, "But death came into the world through the devil's envy" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24). Clement's Greek has the same five words, thanatos eisēlthen eis ton kosmon, which Lake marks as a quotation. Wisdom names phthonos, "envy"; Clement names zēlos, "jealousy", and his next example, Cain, shows how. Paul uses a similar phrase for sin and death through Adam (Romans 5:12).
r: Wisdom of Solomon 2:24; Romans 5:12; Genesis 4:8; 1 John 3:12

a: For it is written like this
t: Cain and Abel in the Greek Bible
p: Clement quotes Genesis 4:3-8 almost word for word from the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew.
b: The quotation follows the Greek Genesis closely; Clement writes "to God" where the Septuagint has "to the Lord". Three things differ from the site's Genesis 4, made from the Hebrew. Cain is "deeply hurt" where the Hebrew says his anger burned. Verses 4:4-5 give the Greek form of Genesis 4:6-7, and Genesis 4:7 is a hard verse in Hebrew (see the note at 4:4). And 4:6 has Cain's words "Let us go out into the open country", which the site's Genesis 4:8 also includes. Hebrews 11:4 and 1 John 3:12 tell the story with other emphases; Clement uses it for one point, jealousy.

a: did not divide it rightly
p: The Greek reads Genesis 4:7 as a fault in how Cain divided his offering. Lightfoot judged the Greek wrong.
b: The site's Genesis 4:7, from the Hebrew, reads: "If you do well, will there not be a lifting up? But if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, but you must rule over it." The Greek is a different sentence. Lightfoot judged that the Septuagint, "which Clement here follows, must be wrong". Its translators seem to have taken "lifting up" as making an offering, and he thought it "more probable" that they read a Hebrew word for cutting up a sacrifice in place of "at the door" (see the variant at Genesis 4:7). So in Greek Cain sinned by not dividing his offering rightly; Lightfoot points to Philo, for whom Cain kept the best for himself. In 4:5 the Greek autou can mean "him" or "it", so the one who "will turn to you" may be Abel, Cain's younger brother, or, as in the Hebrew ("Its desire is for you"), the sin itself. The Plain English Translation keeps "he" and "him", as Lake's English does.
orig: ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς (orthōs de mē dielēs)

a: jealousy and envy led to a brother's murder
p: Clement lists seven examples from Scripture of what jealousy did, then turns to his own day.
b: From Cain to David there are seven: Cain (4:1-7), Jacob (4:8), Joseph (4:9), Moses (4:10), Aaron and Miriam (4:11), Dathan and Abiram (4:12), David (4:13). Chapter 5 then turns to "our own generation": Peter, Paul, the many martyrs and the women (5:1-6:2). Such lists of examples were a common teaching form, Greek and Jewish; Hebrews 11 has a list of examples of faith, and Clement himself makes more lists of the obedient (9-12) and the humble (17-18). Here every example shows jealousy turning brother against brother, the very thing at Corinth.

a: Jacob our father ran away
p: Jacob fled because Esau held a grudge after the stolen blessing.
b: Genesis 27:41-45 tells how Esau hated Jacob for taking the blessing and planned to kill him, so Rebekah sent Jacob away to Haran. Here the jealousy is Esau's. Lake's margin points to Genesis 27:41. Clement calls Jacob "our father", as a church that counts Israel's fathers as its own (compare Romans 4:1 and 1 Corinthians 10:1).

a: Jealousy made Joseph a hunted man
p: The Greek Genesis says Joseph's brothers were jealous of him, the same word Stephen uses.
b: The Septuagint of Genesis 37:11 says "his brothers were jealous of him" (ezēlōsan), and Stephen says the same in Acts: "Out of jealousy the patriarchs sold Joseph away into Egypt" (Acts 7:9). The brothers first meant to kill him (Genesis 37:18-20), then sold him as a slave (Genesis 37:28).

a: Who put you in charge as judge or arbiter over us?
p: The words of the Hebrew who rejected Moses, close to the Greek Exodus and Stephen's speech.
b: The Greek Exodus, followed exactly by Acts 7:27-28, reads "Who put you in charge as ruler and judge over us? You don't mean to kill me, do you, the same way you killed that Egyptian yesterday?" Clement has "judge or arbiter" (kritēn ē dikastēn) where the Greek Bible has "ruler and judge"; the rest matches. Stephen used the scene to show Israel rejecting the one God sent (Acts 7:35). Clement uses it for a church rejecting its leaders. Exodus says Moses fled from Pharaoh (Exodus 2:15); Clement blames it on his own people's jealousy.

a: Aaron and Miriam had to spend their nights outside the camp
p: Numbers says Miriam alone was shut out of the camp. Clement includes Aaron.
b: Aaron and Miriam spoke against Moses (Numbers 12:1-2). The LORD's anger burned "against them" (Numbers 12:9), but only Miriam was struck with skin disease and shut outside the camp for seven days (Numbers 12:10-15). Clement's "Aaron and Miriam" says more than Numbers does about who was put out. His point stands on what Numbers does say: jealousy of a leader God had chosen.

a: Jealousy sent Dathan and Abiram down living into Hades
p: They went down alive into the grave (Numbers 16). A psalm calls their sin jealousy.
b: Numbers 16 tells how Dathan and Abiram joined Korah's rebellion against Moses, and the earth opened and they went down alive to Sheol (Numbers 16:30-33), which the Greek calls Hades. Psalm 106 names the cause: "They grew jealous of Moses in the camp ... The earth split open and swallowed Dathan; it closed over the community of Abiram" (Psalm 106:16-17). Clement calls Moses God's therapōn, "attendant", the Greek of Numbers 12:7 and of Hebrews 3:5. Korah's revolt against God's chosen leaders is the closest Bible parallel to Corinth, and the letter returns to it (43:1-6; 51:3-4).

a: the foreigners
p: Allophyloi, the Greek Bible's usual name for the Philistines.
b: The Septuagint regularly renders "Philistines" as allophyloi, "people of another tribe". Clement uses that word. Clement does not say how the foreigners showed their envy. The jealousy that hunted David was Saul's: "Saul eyed David with suspicion from that day forward" (1 Samuel 18:9).

a: the athletes closest to our own time
p: The image of the games, at home in Corinth, which hosted the Isthmian Games.
b: Clement calls the martyrs "athletes" and says they "kept up the contest" (5:2; Greek athleō). Corinth ran the Isthmian Games, and Paul had used the image to the same church: "on a race course everyone runs, but only one gets the prize" (1 Corinthians 9:24). The prize, the course, the arena and the contest return in 5:5, 6:2 and 7:1. "Our own generation" also helps date the letter: Peter and Paul are recent, but in the past (see the note on 1:1).

a: pillars
p: Paul called James, Cephas and John "pillars"; Clement gives the title to Peter and Paul.
b: In Galatians 2:9 Paul speaks of "James, Cephas and John, who are counted as pillars". Clement uses the image for the apostles he is about to name, Peter and Paul, both of whom the Corinthians knew by name (1 Corinthians 1:12). The church as a building with pillars is also in 1 Timothy 3:15 and Revelation 3:12.

a: Having borne his witness so
p: The verb means "testify". Lightfoot argues that here, for Peter and Paul, it means dying for the faith.
b: Martyreō is "to bear witness". In this era it had not yet become the fixed word for dying for the faith: the martyrs of Gaul in AD 177, as Eusebius quotes their letter, refused the title and kept it for those already dead (Church History 5.2, quoted by Lightfoot). Still, Lightfoot holds that Clement means martyrdom here: the examples are men who contended "until death" (5:2); the word stands in an emphatic place; Hegesippus uses the same phrase of the death of James; and Dionysius of Corinth says Peter and Paul "bore witness at the same time". The site keeps "bore his witness", as in Revelation 2:13 and Acts 22:20, so the reader sees the word.

a: There was Peter
t: What the chapter says about Peter
p: Peter suffered many hardships and died a witness. The chapter names no city and no manner of death.
b: The account is brief. It says he suffered "because of unrighteous jealousy", whose it does not say, and that he went "to the place of glory owed to him". It does not name Rome or a cross. Rome is implied by what follows: the many martyrs were gathered to "these men" and became an example "among us" (6:1), that is, Lightfoot says, among the Roman Christians, in Nero's persecution. John 21:18-19 already points to Peter's death. Lightfoot notes that Polycarp copies the phrase "the place owed" (Polycarp to the Philippians 9:2).
r: 6:1; John 21:18-19; 2 Peter 1:14; Acts 1:25; Polycarp to the Philippians 9:2

a: the prize that endurance wins
p: Brabeion, Paul's word for the victor's prize.
b: Lightfoot notes that brabeion is Paul's own word: "only one gets the prize" (1 Corinthians 9:24) and "I run hard toward the mark, after the prize" (Philippians 3:14). It passed into Latin as bravium. Clement makes Paul the one who "showed the way" to it, by enduring.

a: Seven times he wore chains
p: No New Testament book gives the number. Clement had another source, or counts in his own way.
b: Paul says he was "in more prisons" than his rivals (2 Corinthians 11:23), and Acts tells of arrests at Philippi, Jerusalem, Caesarea and Rome. Lightfoot notes that before 2 Corinthians Acts records only the jailing at Philippi, so Clement must have had his information from some other source; he rejects the idea that the seven come from adding Paul's five floggings (2 Corinthians 11:24). "Banished" fits Paul's flights from Damascus, Pisidian Antioch, Thessalonica and other towns, and "stoned" is Lystra (Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:25, "Once I was stoned"). Paul calls himself a "herald" (1 Timothy 2:7; 2 Timothy 1:11).
r: 2 Corinthians 11:23-27; Acts 9:23-25; Acts 14:19; Acts 16:23-24; 1 Timothy 2:7; 2 Timothy 1:11

a: came to the far limit of the West
t: "The far limit of the West": Spain?
p: Lightfoot argued for Spain, which Paul planned to visit (Romans 15:24, 28). He lists other readings and their holders.
b: To terma tēs dyseōs is "the boundary of the West". Lightfoot shows that Greek and Latin writers used such phrases for the far west of Spain (Strabo; Velleius Paterculus), and finds it "incredible" that a writer in Rome would call Rome itself "the extreme west". Those who hold that Paul died at the end of the Roman captivity, he says, must take it as Rome. He takes it as evidence that Paul made the trip to Spain he had planned (Romans 15:24, 28), after a release from the imprisonment of Acts 28, and quotes the Muratorian Fragment on "the departure of Paul from the city ... to Spain". He lists other readings: "to his extreme limit towards the west" (Baur, Schenkel), "to the sunset of his labours" (Reuss), "the boundary between the east and west" (Schrader, Hilgenfeld), "the goal or centre of the west" (Matthies), and "before the supreme power of the west" (Wieseler, Schaff). Acts ends with Paul in Rome and says nothing of Spain.

a: before the rulers
p: Paul's final witness was given before Roman authorities. The letter names none of them.
b: Lightfoot notes that scholars have proposed names, Nero and his freedman Helius, or the praetorian prefects of AD 67, but "in the absence of information it is waste of time to speculate". He also argues that the words need not mean Paul's trial took place in the far west: "came to the far limit of the West" explains how he taught "the whole world", and the trial comes after. Jesus had told his followers, "Because of me you will even be taken before governors and kings, as evidence to them and to the Gentiles" (Matthew 10:18).

a: the greatest model of endurance for others to trace
p: Hypogrammos was the outline a pupil traced over in learning to write. 1 Peter 2:21 uses it of Christ.
b: Lightfoot: "a copy, an example, as for instance a pencil drawing to be traced over in ink or an outline to be filled in". The site's 1 Peter 2:21 renders it "a model to trace": Christ "left behind for you a model to trace, so that you would follow in his tracks". Clement uses the word again of Christ's humility (16:17) and of the Lord's example in good works (33:8). Here Paul himself is the outline to trace, as Paul told the Corinthians, "Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ" (1 Corinthians 11:1).

a: a great multitude of the chosen
p: Lightfoot links this "great multitude" with the Christians Nero killed at Rome after the fire of AD 64.
b: The many martyrs are joined to Peter and Paul, as their contemporaries, and they suffered "among us", that is, at Rome. Lightfoot takes them to be chiefly the victims of Nero, whose tortures Tacitus describes (Annals 15.44), and he notes that Tacitus's phrase multitudo ingens, "a huge multitude", is the exact counterpart of Clement's "great multitude". Revelation also sees "a crowd so large that no one could count it" of those who came out of the great trouble (Revelation 7:9, 14).

a: as Danaids and Dirces
p: Perhaps Christian women forced to act out myths in the arena as they were killed. The text may be corrupt.
b: In Greek myth the Danaids, the daughters of Danaus, killed their husbands and were punished in the underworld, and Dirce was tied to a bull and dragged to her death. Lightfoot explains the phrase, if it is right, by the cruel shows of Nero's time in which condemned people were put to death in the character of a figure from legend (he cites Suetonius, Nero 11-12, Tertullian, Apology 15, and Martial's On the Spectacles). Dirce's death would fit such a show; the Danaids, he says, are hard to fit at all. All the witnesses have the words, but Lake thinks the text "perhaps corrupt: but no satisfactory emendation is known" (see the variant for the best-known proposal).

a: though their bodies were weak
p: Women, counted weak in body, won the same prize as the apostles.
b: Ancient writers often called women the weaker sex (compare 1 Peter 3:7, "a weaker vessel"). Clement's point is that faith, not bodily strength, finished the race: these women won "a noble prize", the word used of a victor's honor. Later Christian writers made the same point about women and girls among the martyrs; Lightfoot quotes Augustine, Leo and Minucius Felix.

a: This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh
p: Adam's words over Eve, from the Greek Genesis. Jealousy undoes the bond of marriage.
b: The site's Genesis 2:23 reads, "This one at last is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh". The Greek has "this now" (touto nyn), and Clement quotes the Greek. Jealousy "turned wives away from their husbands": Clement does not say how. He may mean marriages broken up by rivalry, or households split when one partner became a Christian and the other did not, as in 1 Corinthians 7:12-16. The text does not settle it.

a: We stand in the same arena
p: Skamma, the dug-out ground marked off for a contest of wrestlers or jumpers.
b: Lightfoot explains skamma as "the ground marked out by digging a trench ... for the arena of a contest", used figuratively by Polybius and Epictetus and often by Christian writers. The church of Rome does not write from a safe distance: "we" are in the same contest. It is a gentle way to correct another church, putting the writers under the same warning (compare Galatians 6:1).

a: the rule handed down to us
p: Kanōn, a measuring rod or standard; paradosis, what is handed on. Later writers speak of "the rule of faith".
b: The Greek is literally "the rule of our tradition". A kanōn is a straight rod for measuring, then a standard (Galatians 6:16; 2 Corinthians 10:13-16). Paradosis is what is handed on, as in Paul's "hold on to the traditions" (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Corinthians 11:2). Clement means the received teaching and way of life of the churches, not yet a list of books. How tradition and Scripture relate is argued between the churches; see the topic page.

a: the blood of Christ
p: Precious to the Father and poured out for salvation, as 1 Peter and the Gospels say.
b: 1 Peter calls it "blood of great worth ... the blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:19), using the same adjective timios. "Poured out" is the word of Jesus at the Last Supper: "this is my blood of the covenant. It is being poured out for many" (Matthew 26:28). Clement draws a practical point: if Christ's blood brought repentance to the whole world, the Corinthians too can repent. The scarlet sign of Rahab returns to the same blood (12:7).

a: the gift of repentance
p: Repentance is God's gift (charis), not only a human act, as in Acts 5:31 and 11:18.
b: The Greek is metanoias charin, "grace of repentance". The site renders metanoia "repentance": a turning of the mind and life. Acts also calls it God's gift: God raised Jesus "so that Israel might be given repentance" (Acts 5:31), and "God has given even the Gentiles repentance that brings life!" (Acts 11:18). Chapters 7-8 build a case that God has always offered it.

a: a place for repentance
p: The phrase of Wisdom of Solomon 12:10 and Hebrews 12:17.
b: The Greek metanoias topos, "a place of repentance", is a Jewish Greek idiom for an opportunity to repent. The Wisdom of Solomon says God "gave them room for repentance" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:10), and Lake's margin points there. Hebrews says of Esau, "He found no place for repentance, though he searched for it with tears" (Hebrews 12:17). Clement's emphasis is the opposite of Hebrews: in every generation the place was open.

a: Noah preached repentance
p: Genesis does not say Noah preached. 2 Peter calls him "a herald of righteousness".
b: Genesis tells that Noah built the ark and obeyed, but records no preaching (Genesis 6-8). 2 Peter 2:5 calls him "a herald of righteousness", and 1 Peter 3:20 speaks of God's patience "in the days of Noah". Clement goes a step further: Noah preached repentance and those who obeyed were saved. Genesis says only Noah's family entered the ark (Genesis 7:1, 7), so Clement's line goes beyond what Genesis says. 9:4 adds that he preached "a new birth to the world".

a: won God's mercy
p: Exilaskomai, the Greek Bible's word for making atonement. Nineveh's prayers turned God's anger.
b: The verb exilaskomai is used in the Greek Leviticus for the priest's work on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Clement uses it of Gentiles who prayed and fasted: by their pleading they "appeased" God. Jonah 3:5-10 tells it: the city believed God, fasted, turned from violence, and God changed his mind about the harm. Jesus pointed to them: "when Jonah preached they repented" (Matthew 12:41). They were "strangers to God" (compare Ephesians 2:12), yet they received salvation.

a: Those who served God's grace
p: Leitourgoi, public servants; the word family behind "liturgy". Here: the prophets.
b: In Greek cities a leitourgia was a public service paid for by a citizen; in the Greek Bible it is the priests' service in the sanctuary. The site renders the family "serve / service" (gloss: "public worship service, the word behind 'liturgy'"). Here the "servants of God's grace" are the prophets, who spoke through the Holy Spirit. Clement uses the same words for Noah's "service" (9:4), the winds' "service" (20:10), and, at length, for the ordered worship of Israel and the church (40:1-44:6).

a: As I live, says the Lord
p: God's oath from Ezekiel, in a form close to how Clement of Alexandria later quotes it.
b: The site's Ezekiel 33:11 reads, "As surely as I live, the Lord GOD declares, I take no pleasure in the death of a wicked man. I take pleasure when a wicked man turns back from his way and lives." The Greek has "the ungodly" and "as that the ungodly turn". Clement's form, "the sinner's death so much as his repentance", is shorter, and Lightfoot notes that Clement of Alexandria quotes the same form (Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved? 39).

a: Repent, house of Israel, of your lawlessness
p: No known book has these words. Lightfoot proposed a lost writing under Ezekiel's name.
b: Parts recall Ezekiel 18:30, Isaiah 1:18, Psalm 103:11 and Jeremiah 3:19 ("you would call me 'My Father'"), but "redder than scarlet and blacker than sackcloth" is in no Bible. Lightfoot weighs two answers: Clement blended several passages, as he often does; or he quotes a lost book under Ezekiel's name. He prefers the second, since Clement of Alexandria quotes part of these words and says "through Ezekiel" (Instructor 1.10), and Clement here treats the lines as one speech of God. The site lists such a book as the Apocryphon of Ezekiel.
r: Ezekiel 18:30-32; Isaiah 1:18; Jeremiah 3:19-22; Psalm 103:10-11; Apocryphon of Ezekiel

a: Rescue the one who is wronged
p: Clement quotes the Greek Isaiah, which differs from the Hebrew in several lines.
b: Where the Greek agrees with the Hebrew, the site's Isaiah 1 wording is used ("Learn how to do good. Go after justice."). Where it differs, Clement's Greek is translated. The Hebrew says "Get the evil you do out from before my eyes"; the Greek adds "out of your souls". The Hebrew "Put the ruthless in their place" is in Greek "Rescue the one who is wronged". The Hebrew "like snow they will turn white" is in Greek "I will make them as white as snow": God himself does the washing. "In another place" introduces a second prophet's words as the same Lord speaking.

a: his death was never found
p: The Greek Genesis and Hebrews say Enoch "was not found" because God took him.
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 5:24 says "Then he was gone, for God took him"; the Greek says "he was not found, because God transferred him", and Hebrews quotes it: "he was not found, because God had carried him off" (Hebrews 11:5). Clement turns it around: Enoch was not found, and neither was his death. Sirach calls him "a pattern of repentance for the generations" (Sirach 44:16); Clement makes him a pattern of obedience. 1 Enoch, a book the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts as Scripture, gives him a long life of visions.

a: a new birth to the world
p: Palingenesia, rebirth: the world after the flood began again, a picture of the world to come.
b: Palingenesia is used twice in the New Testament: of the world "born again" when the Son of Man takes his throne (Matthew 19:28) and of baptism, "the bath of new birth" (Titus 3:5). Noah preached that the world would begin again. Clement adds a touch of his own: the animals went into the ark "together in harmony", the first sign of the letter's great theme (20:1-11).

a: who was called "the friend,"
p: Abraham is called God's friend in Isaiah, Chronicles and James.
b: 2 Chronicles 20:7 speaks of "the offspring of your friend Abraham", and Isaiah 41:8 of "Abraham, who loved me". James says "he was called the friend of God" (James 2:23), right after quoting Genesis 15:6, which Clement quotes at 10:6. Clement repeats the title at 17:2. In James and here the title comes with faith shown in obedience.

a: and you will be blessed
p: The Greek says "you will be blessed" where the Hebrew says "be a blessing".
b: The site's Genesis 12:1-3, from the Hebrew, is used where the Greek agrees. Three lines differ. The Hebrew "And be a blessing!" is in the Greek "and you will be blessed". The Hebrew "whoever treats you with contempt I will curse" uses two different verbs; the Greek has "curse" twice. "All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you" is in Greek "all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in you", close to the forms Paul and Peter quote (Galatians 3:8; Acts 3:25). Clement writes "Go away" (apelthe) where the Septuagint has "Go out".

a: north and south, east and west
p: The Greek has "southwest wind" and "sea", the Hebrew "toward the Negev" and "toward the sea".
b: In Genesis 13:14 the Hebrew directions are "north, Negev, east, sea": the Negev desert lies south of Canaan, and the Mediterranean west. The Greek gives lips, the southwest wind, for the Negev and keeps thalassa, "sea". The site renders both as plain compass points. In 10:5 the Greek also has "sand" where the Hebrew of Genesis 13:16 has "dust"; Genesis 22:17 has both "stars" and "sand".
orig: πρὸς βορρᾶν καὶ λίβα καὶ ἀνατολὰς καὶ θάλασσαν

a: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness
p: The verse Paul and James both use. Clement sets it inside a story of obedience.
b: Genesis 15:6 in the Greek is quoted word for word in Romans 4:3: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Paul uses it to show justification by faith apart from works (Romans 4:1-5); James uses it with the offering of Isaac: "his faith was at work along with his works" (James 2:22). Clement frames it with obedience (10:1, 2, 7) and joins faith to hospitality (10:7). He will later say that we are justified not through ourselves but through faith (32:4). How these fit together is argued between the churches; see the faith and works cards at Romans 3 and James 2.

a: Because of his faith and hospitality he was given a son
p: Clement ties Isaac's birth to Abraham's welcome of the three visitors (Genesis 18).
b: In Genesis 18:1-10 Abraham runs to welcome three strangers, feeds them, and hears the promise that Sarah will have a son. Hebrews 13:2 says that "by this some people have had angels as guests". Clement draws the link: the son was given "because of faith and hospitality", the pair that also saves Lot and Rahab (11:1; 12:1). Then, in obedience, Abraham offered Isaac (Genesis 22; Hebrews 11:17; James 2:21).

a: Lot, because of his hospitality and godliness, was saved out of Sodom
p: Genesis 19 shows Lot taking in strangers; 2 Peter calls him righteous.
b: Lot welcomed the two visitors into his house at Sodom and protected them (Genesis 19:1-3). 2 Peter calls him "righteous" and says God rescued him (2 Peter 2:7-8), and Wisdom of Solomon 10:6 says Wisdom "rescued a righteous man while the ungodly were being destroyed". Clement's lesson: God "does not abandon those who hope in him", and he punishes "those who turn aside", literally "who lean the other way" (heteroklineis).
r: Genesis 19:1-29; 2 Peter 2:6-9; Wisdom of Solomon 10:6; Luke 17:28-30

a: she became a pillar of salt to this day
p: A warning sign for every generation, as in Wisdom of Solomon and Luke.
b: Genesis says only that she looked back and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). The Wisdom of Solomon calls it "a pillar of salt still standing, the monument of a soul that would not believe" (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7), and Jesus said, "Remember Lot's wife!" (Luke 17:32). Clement reads her as "not in harmony" with her husband: she "thought differently" (heterognōmōn), the opposite of the harmony he urges at Corinth.

a: the double-minded
p: Dipsychos, "two-souled", the word of James 1:8.
b: Dipsychos is the word of James: the doubter "is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:8; James 4:8). Clement uses it here with "those who doubt God's power", and again with an unknown Scripture on the double-minded (23:2-3).

a: Rahab the prostitute was saved
p: Hebrews praises her faith, James her works. Clement says faith and hospitality.
b: Hebrews: "By faith Rahab the prostitute was not destroyed along with the disobedient, since she had taken in the spies in peace" (Hebrews 11:31). James: "Rahab the prostitute was the same. She took in the messengers and sent them away by a different road. Was she not justified by works?" (James 2:25). Clement's "faith and hospitality" holds both. Matthew lists her among the ancestors of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). See the faith and works card at Joshua 2.

a: Joshua son of Nun had sent spies to Jericho
p: Clement tells the story in his own words, close to Joshua 2 but not quoting it.
b: The retelling follows Joshua 2 with small changes. Joshua 2:6 says she hid the men on the roof under the flax; Clement says "the upper room". Her confession is shortened: "the Lord God is giving this land into your hands" (compare Joshua 2:9, 11), and the spies' promise is put in their mouths (Joshua 2:14, 18-19). Clement adds a detail Joshua implies, that she "pointed them the wrong way". Lightfoot notes that this retelling is looser than Clement's quotation of Jesus' words in 13:2.

a: she was to hang out something scarlet from her house
t: The scarlet sign and the blood of the Lord
p: Clement reads Rahab's scarlet as a sign of redemption by the Lord's blood. Justin, Irenaeus and Origen took it up.
b: In Joshua 2:18-21 the cord of scarlet thread marks her house to be spared. Clement says the spies made it "plain that through the blood of the Lord there will be redemption": an Old Testament object read as a figure of Christ. Lightfoot traces the reading on, to Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 111), Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.20.12) and Origen's homilies on Joshua: "From this time forward it becomes a common type with the fathers." He suggests that Hebrews 9:19 may have prompted it, where Moses took "the blood of the calves and the goats, along with water, scarlet wool and hyssop". The Syriac version reads "the blood of Christ" (see the variant).
r: Joshua 2:18-21; Hebrews 9:19; Exodus 12:13; Epistle of Barnabas 7:8

a: the woman had not only faith but prophecy
p: Clement calls her act a prophecy. Origen later said the prostitute became a prophet.
b: For Clement the sign meant more than the spies knew: it foretold the Lord's blood (12:7). Lightfoot quotes Origen's homily on Joshua: "from a prostitute she is made a prophet". Joshua 2 itself tells of a woman bargaining for her family's lives; Clement sees in her sign a prophecy without words. Either way her faith stands, which Hebrews 11:31 praises.

a: A wise person should not boast about his wisdom
p: Clement's form follows the Greek prayer of Hannah, which adds Jeremiah's words, and Paul's "boast in the Lord".
b: The site's Jeremiah 9:23 is used for the first lines. The ending is not Jeremiah's. The Greek of Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:10) adds the same three lines and then "let the one who boasts boast in this, to understand and know the Lord, and to do justice and righteousness". Clement's "by seeking him out and doing justice and righteousness" stands close to that Greek. His "let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" is Paul's short form: "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17), written to the same church. Clement says "the Holy Spirit says", as he does when quoting the prophets.

a: keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus
p: The formula of Acts 20:35, used to introduce sayings of Jesus.
b: Paul at Miletus: "we must keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 20:35). Clement uses the same formula (Greek tōn logōn tou kyriou Iēsou) here and at 46:7. It suggests sayings of Jesus were remembered and quoted as a group with authority. The "forbearance" he taught is epieikeia, giving way instead of pressing one's rights (see 1:2). The site renders it "forbearance / forbearing" through the Apostolic Fathers, as its Titus 3:2 has "They should be forbearing" (epieikeis). Its New Testament renders the word three ways, though: "Let all people come to know your gentle fairness" (Philippians 4:5, to epieikes), and "the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:1), where "gentleness" is epieikeia and "meekness" is praütēs, the word Titus 3:2 calls "gentleness". In 1 Clement one English word follows the one Greek word.

a: Show mercy, so that mercy will be shown to you
t: Where did Clement get these sayings?
p: Seven short sayings, all close to Matthew and Luke but in no Gospel in this form.
b: Each line has a Gospel parallel: "mercy will be shown to them" (Matthew 5:7); forgiveness (Matthew 6:14; Luke 6:37); doing as you would be done by (Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31); giving (Luke 6:38); judging (Matthew 7:1-2); and "The measure you use is the one that will be used to measure out to you" (Matthew 7:2; Luke 6:38). "As you show kindness" has no exact parallel; Lightfoot notes Justin quotes Luke 6:36 as "be kind and compassionate". Lightfoot held that Clement quotes Matthew and Luke loosely, as he does Scripture elsewhere, and so "the hypothesis ... that Clement derived the saying from oral tradition or from some lost Gospel, is not needed". Polycarp gives a similar list (Polycarp to the Philippians 2:3), probably from Clement, Lightfoot says, and Clement of Alexandria quotes it almost exactly (Stromata 2.18).
r: Matthew 5:7; Matthew 6:14-15; Matthew 7:1-2; Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31; Luke 6:36-38; Polycarp to the Philippians 2:3

a: trembles at my sayings
p: Clement's Greek has "gentle" where the Greek Isaiah has "lowly", and "sayings" for "words".
b: The site's Isaiah 66:2, from the Hebrew, reads "But this is the one I will look to: the poor one, stricken in spirit, who trembles at my word." The Greek Isaiah has "the lowly and quiet one who trembles at my words". Clement writes "gentle" (praüs, the word of Matthew 5:5 and 11:29) and "my sayings" (ta logia, the word of Romans 3:2, "the oracles of God"). The change fits his point: the humble, not the boastful, are the ones God regards. "The holy word says" treats Isaiah as God's own speech.

a: for us to obey God rather than
p: The principle of the apostles in Acts, turned here against leaders of a church faction.
b: Peter and John asked, "Is it right before God to heed you rather than God?" (Acts 4:19), and the apostles said, "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). In Acts the people are the Temple rulers; in Clement they are "the leaders" (archēgoi, "leaders, ringleaders") of the revolt. The same word names them again at 51:1.

a: The land will be home for the kind
p: Clement's lines blend the Greek Proverbs 2:21-22 with Psalm 37 and put "the kind" first.
b: Lake's margin gives both Proverbs 2:21-22 and Psalm 37:9 and 38 (36:9 and 36:38 in the Greek numbering). The site's Proverbs 2:21-22 reads, "The land will be home for upright people, and the wholehearted will be left in it, but from the land the wicked will be cut off". The Greek Proverbs has "the upright" (eutheis), "the holy" (hosioi) and "will be driven out" (exōsthēsontai). Clement's last line takes its verb from the Greek Psalm: his "the lawbreakers will be destroyed" (hoi de paranomountes exolethreuthēsontai) stands beside Psalm 36:38, hoi de paranomoi exolethreuthēsontai (the site's Psalm 37:38: "But rebels will be destroyed all together"). In the first line he has chrēstoi, "the kind", and akakoi, "the innocent". "The kind" picks up the call he has just made, "Let us show kindness" (chrēsteusōmetha, 14:3).

a: the man of peace has a remnant left to him
p: The Greek Psalm has "cedars of Lebanon" and "a remnant for the man of peace".
b: The site's Psalm 37:35-37, from the Hebrew, has "spreading himself out like a lush tree in its native soil", "But he passed on", and "the man of peace has a future". The Greek reads "lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon", "I went past", and "there is a remnant for the man of peace". Clement quotes the Greek but rewords one line: the Greek Psalm has "I looked for him, and his place was not found", and Clement has "I looked for the place where he had been, and I did not find it". The verse ends on the word that leads into chapter 15: peace.

a: those who want peace only as a pretense
p: Not every call for peace is real. Clement contrasts peace rooted in godliness with peace as a cover.
b: The Greek contrasts those who "make peace with godliness" and those who "want peace with hypocrisy". Clement does not say who is meant. It may be a warning against the faction's own talk of peace, or against anyone in the church who wants quiet without repentance. The proof texts that follow all set lips against hearts (15:2-5). Jeremiah had warned of prophets who healed the people's wound lightly, saying there was peace when there was none (Jeremiah 6:14).

a: This people gives me honor with their lips
p: Clement quotes the short form found in Mark 7:6 and Matthew 15:8, not the Greek Isaiah.
b: The Greek Isaiah reads "This people draws near to me with their mouth, and with their lips they honor me, but their heart is far from me". Mark 7:6 and Matthew 15:8 have a shorter form, "This people gives me honor with their lips, but their heart keeps far away from me". Clement has that shorter form, with one difference: "is far away" (apestin) for "keeps far away" (apechei). So he may quote a Gospel, or a short form known in the churches. 2 Clement 3:5 has the same short form with the same apestin, but credits it to Isaiah: "He also says in Isaiah". "Somewhere it says" (legei gar pou) is a way of quoting Scripture also found in Hebrews 2:6.

a: They loved him with their mouth
p: The Hebrew says they flattered God; the Greek says they "loved" him with their mouth.
b: The site's Psalm 78:36-37 reads "But they sweet-talked him with their mouths, and with their tongues they lied to him. Their hearts were not firm with him, and they did not keep true to his covenant." The Greek has "they loved him with their mouth". 15:3 is likewise Psalm 62:4 in Greek. The site's Psalm 62:4, from the Hebrew, has "With their mouth they bless, but in their inner parts they curse"; the Greek (Psalm 61:5 there) has "heart" (kardia) where the Hebrew has "inner parts", and Clement follows the Greek. Clement strings Psalms together on one theme, mouth against heart, a common way of teaching from Scripture.

a: Who is lord over us?
p: Two psalms joined by the words "lying lips". The proud say, "Who is lord over us?"
b: The first line is Psalm 31:18 ("Let lying lips be struck dumb, lips that speak against the righteous"), the rest Psalm 12:3-5 in Greek. The Hebrew of Psalm 12:4 ends "Who can be our master?"; the Greek is "Who is our lord?" At Corinth the question would sound like the faction that would not accept its elders. In Psalm 12:5 the LORD rises up for the poor; Clement's Greek ends, "I will speak out boldly for him". On the words that only the Syriac keeps, see the variant.

a: not to those who lift themselves up over his flock
p: The flock belongs to Christ. The rebels at Corinth lifted themselves over it.
b: Paul told the Ephesian elders to watch "the whole flock" (Acts 20:28), and 1 Peter tells elders to "shepherd God's flock ... Do not act as lords over those allotted to you; be patterns for the flock instead" (1 Peter 5:2-3). Clement turns the warning on the faction: Christ belongs to the humble, not to those who exalt themselves. "The flock of Christ" returns where Clement defends the elders (44:3; 54:2; 57:2).

a: The scepter of God's majesty, the Lord Jesus Christ
p: A title for Christ: the rod by which God rules. He came without the show that power brings.
b: A scepter is the king's rod. Psalm 45:6, quoted of the Son in Hebrews 1:8, says "the scepter of fairness is your kingdom's scepter", and Balaam saw that "a scepter will rise from Israel" (Numbers 24:17). Clement calls Christ himself the scepter of God's majesty, and then says he did not come in pomp, "though he could have": the thought of Philippians 2:6-8, where Christ, being in the form of God, emptied himself and made himself low. The Holy Spirit "had spoken about him" in Isaiah 53, which follows.

a: Lord, who has believed what we have heard?
p: The whole song of the suffering servant from the Greek Isaiah. Where it differs from the Hebrew, Clement is translated.
b: Clement quotes Isaiah 53:1-12 entire, very close to the Septuagint, as the Spirit's words "about him", Christ. The Plain English Translation uses the site's Isaiah wording where the Greek agrees, and, in 16:5, 16:7-8 and 16:10, the wording of the New Testament books that quote the same Greek: Acts 8:32-33, 1 Peter 2:22 and 1 Peter 2:24. Where the Greek differs from the Hebrew, Clement's Greek is translated, and the main differences are in the next notes.

a: as of a little child
p: The Greek has "a little child" where the Hebrew has "a little shoot", a plant word.
b: The site's Isaiah 53:2 reads "He came up before him like a little shoot, like a root from parched ground". The Greek reads "We announced, as a child, before him". The Hebrew yoneq here means a young shoot, but the same spelling elsewhere means a nursing child (Deuteronomy 32:25), and the Greek took it that way; for "he came up" it has "we announced". The rest of the verse is close. In 16:3 the Greek also says he "knew how to bear weakness" where the Hebrew says he "knew sickness well".

a: carries our sins
p: The Greek Isaiah 53:4 says he carries our sins. The Hebrew says our sicknesses; Matthew follows the Hebrew.
b: The site's Isaiah 53:4 reads "Yet it was our sicknesses that he carried, our pains that he bore." The Greek has "This one carries our sins and suffers pain for us". The New Testament uses both: Matthew 8:17 quotes the Hebrew sense for Jesus' healings ("He himself took our weaknesses and carried our diseases"), and 1 Peter 2:24 the Greek sense ("He himself carried our sins up in his body onto the tree"). Clement's Greek follows the second.

a: And the Lord handed him over for our sins
p: The Greek verb of Isaiah 53:6, 12, the word the Gospels and Paul use for Jesus being "handed over".
b: The Hebrew of Isaiah 53:6 says "the LORD made the guilt of us all fall on him". The Greek has "the Lord handed him over" (paredōken), and the same verb ends the song, "because of their sins he was handed over" (16:14). It is the word of Romans 4:25, "who was handed over for our trespasses", and of the Gospels' passion story. Clement writes "for our sins" (hyper) where the Septuagint has the dative.

a: And I will give the wicked in return for his burial
p: The Greek Isaiah 53:9-10 differs much from the Hebrew here.
b: The site's Isaiah 53:9-10, from the Hebrew: "They gave him a burial place among the wicked, and, in his deaths, with a rich man ... But the LORD desired to crush him and made him sick." The Greek has God speak: "I will give the wicked in return for his burial and the rich in return for his death", and "the Lord wants to cleanse him of his wound". In 16:11 the Greek has "If you make an offering for sin" (plural "you"), for the Hebrew "If his life is made a guilt offering". "Nor was trickery found in his mouth" is the wording 1 Peter 2:22 uses.

a: he was counted among the lawless
p: Jesus quotes these words of himself at the Last Supper (Luke 22:37).
b: "For I tell you, this scripture must be completed in me: 'And he was counted with the lawless.'" (Luke 22:37). The Greek word Luke and Clement share is anomoi, "lawless people"; the site's Isaiah 53:12, from the Hebrew, says "counted with the rebels". Clement's whole quotation ends where the Greek song ends, with the servant "handed over".

a: But I am a worm and not a man
p: "He himself says": Clement hears Christ speaking in Psalm 22, as the Gospels do.
b: Clement introduces Psalm 22:6-8 with "again he himself says", that is, Christ. The site's Psalm 22:6-7 is used, since the Greek agrees. In Psalm 22:8 the Hebrew has "Roll it onto the LORD!"; the Greek has "He hoped in the Lord", and Clement follows the Greek. The Gospels put these words in the mouths of the crowd at the cross: "He has put his trust in God, so God should get him free now, if he takes delight in him" (Matthew 27:43), with the shaking heads of Matthew 27:39. Jesus himself prays the psalm's first line (Mark 15:34).

a: the yoke of his grace
p: Jesus called his yoke kind. Clement's point: if the Lord was humble, so must we be.
b: Jesus: "Lift my yoke onto yourselves and learn from me, because I am gentle and my heart is humble" (Matthew 11:29). Clement calls it "the yoke of his grace" and draws the lesson in one question, the hinge of chapters 13-19: "If the Lord was so humble, what should we do?" Christ is the "model to trace" (see 5:7).

a: went around in goat hides and sheepskins
p: Clement's words are those of Hebrews 11:37, and he names the prophets Hebrews leaves unnamed.
b: Hebrews 11:37 says the faithful "wandered about dressed in sheepskins and goat hides". Clement's Greek has the same two rare words (mēlōtai, aigeia dermata) and the same verb "went around", and he names whom he means: Elijah, whose cloak the Greek Kings calls a mēlōtē (1 Kings 19:13, 19; 2 Kings 2:8, 13-14), Elisha who took it up, and Ezekiel. This is one of several places where 1 Clement and Hebrews meet; the closest is chapter 36, where the question whether Clement used Hebrews is taken up.

a: those who were given a good witness
p: Martyreomai in the passive: those Scripture speaks well of, as in Hebrews 11:2 and 11:39.
b: The passive of martyreō, "to be witnessed to", means to have a good report. Hebrews uses it of the heroes of faith: "the people of long ago were given a good witness" (Hebrews 11:2; Hebrews 11:39). Clement uses it four times in these chapters: of the great ones in general (17:1), of Abraham (17:2), of David (18:1), and in the summary (19:1). The site keeps one English phrase for all four, so the thread is visible.

a: But I am earth and ashes
p: Abraham's words as he pleads for Sodom. The Greek has "earth", the Hebrew "dust".
b: The site's Genesis 18:27 reads "though I am only dust and ashes". The Greek reads gē kai spodos, "earth and ashes", and Clement quotes the Greek. The setting makes Clement's point: Abraham, God's friend, speaks so while "looking steadily at God's glory".

a: Job was righteous and blameless, true
p: The Greek Job has four words of praise where the Hebrew has two pairs.
b: The site's Job 1:1 reads "The man was wholehearted and upright. He feared God and kept away from evil." The Greek has "true, blameless, righteous, God-revering, keeping away from every evil thing". Clement puts "righteous and blameless" first. Then he quotes Job against himself (17:4), from the Greek of Job 14:4-5: "Who will be clean from filth? Not one, even if his life on earth is one day." The Hebrew of those verses, in the site's wording, is "Who can make what is clean come out of what is unclean? No one can." (Job 14:4).

a: faithful in all his house
p: Numbers 12:7, as used in Hebrews 3. Then Moses' humble words at the burning bush.
b: God says of Moses, "In all my house he is faithful" (Numbers 12:7), and Hebrews compares him with Christ: "Moses was faithful in the whole of God's house as an attendant" (Hebrews 3:5; Hebrews 3:2). At the bush Moses asked, "Who am I to go to Pharaoh?" (Exodus 3:11); Clement shortens it to "Who am I, that you send me?" "Weak of voice and slow of tongue" is the Greek of Exodus 4:10, where the site, from the Hebrew, has "heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue". Numbers 12:3 calls Moses the most humble man on earth.

a: But I am steam from a pot
t: A saying of Moses in no Bible
p: No known book has these words. Lightfoot suggests a lost writing; James 4:14 is the nearest Bible verse.
b: Lightfoot: "This quotation is not found in the Old Testament or in any apocryphal book extant whole or in part." The nearest Bible words are James 4:14, "You are a puff of steam, seen for a moment and then gone" (the same Greek word, atmis), and Hosea 13:3, "like smoke from a window". He mentions Hilgenfeld's view that it comes from the Assumption of Moses (on the site, the Testament of Moses), "not impossible", and adds that the apocryphal work he proposes for 23:3-4 is another from which the words "might well have been taken" (see the note at 23:3); and notes the image is common in Stoic writers such as Seneca and Marcus Aurelius. Clement treats it as Scripture: "And again he says".
r: James 4:14; Hosea 13:3; Psalm 102:3; Testament of Moses; 23:3

a: I have found a man to suit my heart, David son of Jesse
p: Psalm 89:20 and 1 Samuel 13:14 joined, as in Paul's speech in Acts 13:22.
b: The site's Acts 13:22 reads "I have found David son of Jesse, a man to suit my heart". Paul there joins Psalm 89:20 ("I have found David my servant") and 1 Samuel 13:14 ("a man to suit his own heart"), and Clement makes the same join, with "With eternal mercy I have anointed him" for Psalm 89:20's second line. The Hebrew there has "with my holy oil"; Rahlfs's Septuagint has "with my holy oil" too, but the Codex Vaticanus that Swete prints has "with holy mercy" (Greek eleos, "mercy", beside elaion, "oil"). Clement's "eternal mercy" goes with that reading.

a: Have mercy on me, O God, as your mercy is great
p: David's great prayer of repentance, quoted from the Greek almost word for word.
b: Clement quotes Psalm 51:1-17 from the Septuagint, leaving out the heading about Nathan and Bathsheba and the last two verses about Zion. The Plain English Translation uses the site's Psalm 51 wording where the Greek agrees (51:11 is word for word) and Clement's Greek where it differs: "mercy" (eleos) where the Hebrew has hesed, which the site renders "loyal love"; "lawless deed" where the Hebrew has "rebellions". Against the Greek Psalm, Clement's own changes are small: the word order of 18:13, and in 18:15 "mouth" and "lips" the other way around. His lesson is in the frame: even David, "given a good witness", confessed his sin. This and Isaiah 53 are the two longest quotations in the letter.

a: so that you may be proved right in your words, and win your case when you are judged
p: Paul quotes this line of the Greek Psalm 51:4 in Romans; the site's Romans wording is used.
b: Paul: "Let God be true, and every human being a liar, as it is written: 'So that you may be proved right in your words, and win your case when you are judged.'" (Romans 3:4). The Greek of Romans and of Clement is the Septuagint of Psalm 51:4, so the Plain English Translation uses the Romans wording here. The site's Psalm 51:4 from the Hebrew says "So you are in the right when you speak, and clear when you pass judgment".

a: your holy spirit
p: Lowercase, as the site's Psalm 51:11, though Clement's church spoke of the Holy Spirit.
b: The Psalm's "holy spirit" (Hebrew ruach qodsheka) is printed lowercase in the site's Psalm 51:11, so as not to decide how much the psalmist meant. The line here is the same, word for word. Clement himself speaks of "the Holy Spirit" who spoke through the prophets (8:1; 13:1; 16:2). Isaiah 63:10-11 is the only other Old Testament passage with the phrase.

a: a governing spirit
p: Hēgemonikos, a word the Stoics used for the ruling center of the self.
b: The site's Psalm 51:12, from the Hebrew, prays for "a generous spirit" (Hebrew nediva, "willing, noble"). The Greek has pneumati hēgemonikō, "a leading, governing spirit". Lightfoot notes that the Stoics "more especially affected the term" to hēgemonikon for "the principle of life, the centre of being, the seat of the personality". A Greek reader would hear a prayer for a spirit that rules the self.

a: For if you had wanted a sacrifice, I would have given one
p: The Psalm's word that God wants a broken spirit more than offerings, a theme of the prophets and Hebrews.
b: Psalm 51:16-17 stands with Hosea 6:6, Psalm 40:6 and Psalm 50:13-14 in saying that God does not need sacrifices, but a broken and humble heart. Jesus quoted Hosea (Matthew 9:13), and Hebrews 10:5-8 quotes Psalm 40. Clement uses the Psalm for humility, not for an argument about sacrifice; his own church still speaks of offerings and priests as a picture of order (40:1-41:4).

a: his sayings
p: Ta logia, God's spoken words, the Scriptures; "the oracles of God" in Romans 3:2.
b: The site renders ta logia "the oracles" in Romans 3:2 and "living sayings" in Acts 7:38. Clement uses it of the words of Scripture here and at 13:4, 53:1 and 62:3. The generations "before us" who "received his sayings in fear and truth" were made better by the humble examples of their own past, as Christians are now. The thought is close to Hebrews 11:39-12:1.

a: the goal of peace that was handed down to us from the beginning
p: The thesis of the letter in one phrase: peace, handed down from the beginning.
b: Here the letter turns from examples to its goal. Skopos is the mark a runner aims at (Philippians 3:14 uses the same word: "I run hard toward the mark"). Peace is "handed down" (paradedomenon) like the tradition of 7:2. From here to 20:12 Clement shows the whole creation keeping peace and harmony under God, so that a church in revolt is out of step with the world itself. The two halves of the letter meet here: the peace of creation now, the order of the ministry in chapters 40-44.

a: the Father and Maker of the whole world
p: Plato called the cause of the universe its "Maker and Father". Clement calls God "Father and Maker" of the whole world.
b: Clement calls God patēr kai ktistēs, "Father and Maker". Plato's Timaeus (28c) says that "to discover the Maker and Father of this Universe were a task indeed", and that having found him, "to declare Him unto all men were a thing impossible". Clement's God is no hidden craftsman: he is the Father of Jesus Christ (7:4), who made the world, as Genesis says, and keeps it (20:11), and the letter speaks of him to everyone. The shared words show a Christian writer in Rome speaking a language his Greek neighbors knew. Honest verdict: a shared idiom, not dependence on Plato for the doctrine.

a: how free of anger he is toward all that he has made
p: Clement says God is free of anger toward his creation. Elsewhere he speaks of judgment.
b: The Greek word aorgētos, "without anger", was a quality Greek philosophers gave the divine. Clement does not deny judgment: the Master hands those who turn aside over to punishment (11:1), and the sword devours the unwilling (8:4). He means God's patience: his will is "patient" (makrothymos), slow to anger, as Exodus 34:6 says. Later Christian writers argued about how the Bible's language of God's anger fits a God who does not change; Clement only draws the moral that his children should be slow to anger too.

a: The heavens, moving as he directs them, submit to him in peace
t: The cosmos as a lesson in order
p: Clement's hymn to creation draws on Genesis, Job and the Psalms, and on Greek ideas of cosmic order.
b: Chapter 20 is a hymn in prose: the heavens, day and night, sun, moon and stars, the earth, the deeps, the sea and ocean, the seasons, the winds, the springs and the smallest creatures all keep their place "in peace and harmony" (20:11). The Bible's own praise of creation stands behind it (Psalm 104; Psalm 148; Job 38; Jeremiah 31:35-36). So does the Greek and Stoic idea of the universe as a well-ordered whole (kosmos means "order"), where concord holds all things together. Clement's use is moral: if the stars and seas obey their bounds, the church can obey its order.

a: the dancing choirs of stars
p: Choros: a dance, or a band of dancers. The stars move like a chorus in a round.
b: A Greek choros was a group who danced and sang together, as at a festival or in a play. Clement pictures the stars moving like dancers in a round, and uses the picture for the stars' "harmony", and adds that they never stray from their "circuits" (horismoi, "set bounds"). The Bible speaks of the stars as an army God calls by name (Isaiah 40:26) and of the morning stars singing together (Job 38:7).

a: The great hollow of the boundless sea
p: God set bounds for the sea at creation. Clement quotes Job 38:11 in Greek.
b: "Gathered into its pools" echoes the Greek Genesis 1:9, where the water "was gathered into its gatherings" (synagōgai). The "bars set around it" and the quotation in 20:7 come from Job 38:8-11; the site's Job 38:11, from the Hebrew, reads "Up to here you may come, but not one step more. Here a stop is set for your proud waves", and the Greek has "your waves will break within you". Psalm 104:9 and Jeremiah 5:22 praise the same bounds.

a: the worlds beyond it
p: Lands past the ocean that surrounds the known world. Early Christian writers were divided on them.
b: Ancient geography pictured the known world ringed by Ocean. Lightfoot thinks Clement may mean some unknown land in the far west beyond the ocean; he notes that Greek writers from Aristotle on had speculated about such lands, and that Seneca's Medea foretold a day when Ocean would open to a new world. He reports that Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria seem to read the verse so, and that Origen discussed it at length, all accepting these "other worlds"; later Tertullian condemned the idea, and Lactantius mocked the Antipodes (Divine Institutes 3.24). Clement says only that the same Master steers them.

a: hold out their breasts to give people life
p: Mazoi, breasts: the springs nurse humankind like a mother.
b: The Greek mazoi is the plain word for breasts. Clement pictures ever-flowing springs nursing people. The Bible likewise speaks of God's care through water and springs (Psalm 104:10-13; Isaiah 41:18) and of God as a nursing mother (Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 66:11-13). The winds too do their leitourgia, "service" (see 8:1).

a: The great Creator and Master of all things
p: Dēmiourgos, "craftsman", Plato's word for the maker of the world, used here of God.
b: Dēmiourgos meant a craftsman or public worker; Plato used it for the maker of the world in the Timaeus, and from there "demiurge" entered philosophy. The New Testament has it once, of God as the city's "architect and maker" (Hebrews 11:10). Clement uses it often (26:1; 33:2; 35:3; 59:2), always of the one God, with "Master" beside it. Later Gnostic teachers made "the Demiurge" a lesser being apart from the true God; Clement's usage shows how the word sounded before that.

a: us who have fled for refuge to his compassion
p: The image of Hebrews 6:18, where believers have "run to him for safety".
b: Hebrews: "we who have run to him for safety would have strong encouragement to grab hold of the hope that lies ahead of us" (Hebrews 6:18). The picture is of a city of refuge (Numbers 35:11). Clement's order of thought is the letter's: God does good to all things, and above all to the church that has fled to him through Jesus Christ.

a: To him be the glory and the majesty forever and ever. Amen.
p: The first of many doxologies in 1 Clement, in the form of the New Testament letters.
b: "To him be the glory" is the form of Romans 11:36 ("To him be the glory for all the ages. Amen.") and Galatians 1:5. "Majesty" (megalōsynē) is in Jude 1:25 and Hebrews 1:3 ("the Majesty in the heights"). Clement closes many sections this way (38:4; 43:6; 50:7; 61:3; 65:2), and the doxology here ends the first main movement of the letter.
